items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a desert soil with little organic matter, weak horizons and often accumulations of calcium carbonate, gypsum or salts”.
items.answer: Aridisol
items.markingKey: Aridisol: a desert soil with little organic matter, weak horizons and often accumulations of calcium carbonate, gypsum or salts. [1]

items.stem: Explain the formation of aridisols.
items.answer: Low rainfall means little leaching, so salts and carbonates accumulate; high evaporation draws water up by capillary action, depositing calcrete and salts; sparse vegetation gives little humus; weak horizon development.

items.stem: Explain how irrigation can cause salinisation.
items.answer: Water applied in excess raises the water table; capillary rise brings saline groundwater to the surface; evaporation leaves salts; irrigation water also contains dissolved salts; poor drainage prevents flushing.

items.stem: Soil at a farm in the Murray-Darling Basin, Australia has an electrical conductivity (EC) of 12 dS/m. Relative yield (%) = 100 − b × (EC − a) when EC is greater than a, where a is the crop’s salinity threshold (dS/m) and b the % yield loss per dS/m above it. Values: tomato: a = 2.5, b = 9.9; cotton: a = 7.7, b = 5.2; rice: a = 3, b = 12. Suggest how the field could be reclaimed.
items.answer: Install sub-surface drains, then flush salts with good-quality water; switch to drip irrigation; grow salt-tolerant crops; apply gypsum on sodic soils.

items.stem: Soil at a field near the Aral Sea, Uzbekistan has an electrical conductivity (EC) of 6.7 dS/m. Relative yield (%) = 100 − b × (EC − a) when EC is greater than a, where a is the crop’s salinity threshold (dS/m) and b the % yield loss per dS/m above it. Values: rice: a = 3, b = 12; maize: a = 1.7, b = 12; cotton: a = 7.7, b = 5.2. (a) Calculate the expected relative yield of each crop. (b) State which crop the farmer should grow and why.
items.answer: (a) rice: 55.6%; maize: 40%; cotton: 100% (b) Cotton: it is the most salt-tolerant of the three, giving the highest relative yield.

items.stem: “Human activity is the main cause of soil degradation in arid environments.” Discuss.
items.answer: For: Irrigation without drainage causes salinisation and waterlogging (Indus Basin, Aral Sea basin); overgrazing and cultivation expose soil to erosion. Against: Natural salinity, wind erosion of bare soils and drought cause degradation; climate change increases evaporation. Conclusion: Natural conditions make arid soils fragile, but human mismanagement is the main cause of rapid degradation.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “aridisol”?
options: The upward movement of water through soil pores, drawn towards the surface where it evaporates.
The accumulation of soluble salts in the soil, often caused by capillary rise and evaporation of irrigation water.
A desert soil with little organic matter, weak horizons and often accumulations of calcium carbonate, gypsum or salts.
A hard layer of calcium carbonate formed in desert soils by evaporation of water.
items.answer: A desert soil with little organic matter, weak horizons and often accumulations of calcium carbonate, gypsum or salts.

items.answer: Not correct. They lack organic matter and nitrogen and may contain harmful salts.

items.stem: Explain how salinisation can be managed.
items.answer: Efficient irrigation (drip) and less water; drainage to lower the water table; leaching salts with extra water where drainage exists; salt-tolerant crops; planting trees to lower the water table.

items.stem: Explain how xerophytes are adapted to aridity.
items.answer: Small, waxy or spiny leaves and sunken stomata reduce transpiration; water storage in stems; deep tap roots or wide shallow roots; CAM photosynthesis; shedding leaves in drought.

items.stem: Explain the life cycle of desert ephemerals.
items.answer: Seeds stay dormant for years; germination is triggered by enough rain (inhibitors washed out); rapid growth, flowering and seed setting within weeks before the soil dries.

items.stem: Assess the view that plants and animals in hot deserts are adapted more to lack of water than to high temperatures. In your answer you may refer to CAM and xerophytes.

items.stem: Explain how overgrazing leads to land degradation.
items.answer: Livestock remove grass faster than it regrows; trampling compacts soil and reduces infiltration; bare soil is eroded by wind and rain; palatable species disappear and shrubs invade.

items.stem: Outline the evidence that supports, and the evidence that challenges, the view that overgrazing is the main cause of degradation in semi-arid ecosystems.
items.answer: For: Rising herd sizes, sedentarisation and boreholes concentrate grazing, causing loss of cover and erosion (Sahel piospheres). Against: Drought, rainfall variability, expansion of cultivation, fuelwood collection and fire changes also cause degradation; many rangelands recover after droughts (non-equilibrium ecology). Conclusion: Overgrazing is important locally, especially around water points, but rainfall variability and other land uses are also major causes.

items.stem: Explain why traditional nomadic pastoralism was relatively sustainable.
items.answer: Herds moved with the rains, so pasture had time to recover; herd size adjusted to drought; mixed herds used different vegetation.

Values: rice: a = 3, b = 12; cotton: a = 7.7, b = 5.2; tomato: a = 2.5, b = 9.9. (a) Calculate the expected relative yield of each crop. (b) Suggest how the field could be reclaimed.
items.answer: (a) rice: 17.2%; cotton: 88.6%; tomato: 26.7% (b) Install sub-surface drains, then flush salts with good-quality water; switch to drip irrigation; grow salt-tolerant crops; apply gypsum on sodic soils.

items.answer: Not correct. Humps store fat; camels tolerate dehydration and conserve water.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain how xerophytes are adapted to aridity. (b) Explain the life cycle of desert ephemerals.
items.answer: (a) Small, waxy or spiny leaves and sunken stomata reduce transpiration; water storage in stems; deep tap roots or wide shallow roots; CAM photosynthesis; shedding leaves in drought. (b) Seeds stay dormant for years; germination is triggered by enough rain (inhibitors washed out); rapid growth, flowering and seed setting within weeks before the soil dries.

items.stem: “Plants and animals in hot deserts are adapted more to lack of water than to high temperatures.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to animal behaviour, CAM and xerophytes.
items.answer: For: Most adaptations reduce water loss (waxy leaves, CAM, concentrated urine) or obtain water (deep roots, storage, metabolic water). Against: Many adaptations deal with heat (pale colours, nocturnal behaviour, large ears, burrowing); the two stresses are linked since cooling by evaporation uses water. Conclusion: Water shortage is the dominant stress, but adaptations to heat and water are closely linked.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “carrying capacity (grazing)”?
options: The maximum number of livestock an area can support without damaging the vegetation and soil.
A zone of degraded vegetation around a waterhole or borehole, where grazing pressure is highest.
A standard unit for comparing livestock, equivalent to an animal of 250 kg such as a cow.
Grazing by more animals than the land can support, removing vegetation cover and exposing soil.
items.answer: The maximum number of livestock an area can support without damaging the vegetation and soil.
items.markingKey: Carrying capacity (grazing): the maximum number of livestock an area can support without damaging the vegetation and soil. [1]

items.stem: Explain why grazing can be beneficial for semi-arid ecosystems.
items.answer: Moderate grazing stimulates grass growth, recycles nutrients in dung, disperses seeds and reduces fuel for intense fires.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why traditional nomadic pastoralism was relatively sustainable. (b) Explain how overgrazing leads to land degradation.
items.answer: (a) Herds moved with the rains, so pasture had time to recover; herd size adjusted to drought; mixed herds used different vegetation. (b) Livestock remove grass faster than it regrows; trampling compacts soil and reduces infiltration; bare soil is eroded by wind and rain; palatable species disappear and shrubs invade.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that overgrazing is the main cause of degradation in semi-arid ecosystems?
items.answer: For: Rising herd sizes, sedentarisation and boreholes concentrate grazing, causing loss of cover and erosion (Sahel piospheres). Against: Drought, rainfall variability, expansion of cultivation, fuelwood collection and fire changes also cause degradation; many rangelands recover after droughts (non-equilibrium ecology). Conclusion: Overgrazing is important locally, especially around water points, but rainfall variability and other land uses are also major causes.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how irrigation can cause salinisation. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “Salinisation reduces crop yields.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Water applied in excess raises the water table; capillary rise brings saline groundwater to the surface; evaporation leaves salts; irrigation water also contains dissolved salts; poor drainage prevents flushing. (b) Correct. Salts make it harder for plants to absorb water and can be toxic.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the formation of aridisols. (b) Explain how irrigation can cause salinisation.
items.answer: (a) Low rainfall means little leaching, so salts and carbonates accumulate; high evaporation draws water up by capillary action, depositing calcrete and salts; sparse vegetation gives little humus; weak horizon development. (b) Water applied in excess raises the water table; capillary rise brings saline groundwater to the surface; evaporation leaves salts; irrigation water also contains dissolved salts; poor drainage prevents flushing.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that human activity is the main cause of soil degradation in arid environments? In your answer you may refer to management and irrigation.
items.answer: For: Irrigation without drainage causes salinisation and waterlogging (Indus Basin, Aral Sea basin); overgrazing and cultivation expose soil to erosion. Against: Natural salinity, wind erosion of bare soils and drought cause degradation; climate change increases evaporation. Conclusion: Natural conditions make arid soils fragile, but human mismanagement is the main cause of rapid degradation.
